text:
From all the declining revenue charts I’m seeing lately it’s clear indie founders are in trouble. But in most cases it’s not because AI models are directly competing with them. It’s a distribution problem.

The old playbook ran on search traffic. Pump out content, rank for the keywords that matter, convert. That stopped working a while ago but people are only panicking now that it’s showing up in their bottom line.

Today the only way into the top recommendations is building a real brand. Content, people talking about you, video reviews, mentions, signals from every direction. That’s hard even for a great marketer with a team behind them. For a solo, inexperienced founder it’s brutal.

Social can help but on its own it can’t replace the volume + intent combo search used to deliver. I don’t know where this goes from here but my guess is fewer one man shows and more teams of two: technical founder and marketing cofounder.

text:
A successful AI project has nothing to do with AI.
I learned that the expensive way.

My firm was the first AI development company built for advertising and marketing agencies. We've put tens of thousands of hours into 
AI projects for our clients.

The #1 thing that surprises every client is simple:

The AI was never the hard part.

Successful projects come down to one thing. Clear objectives, tied to the company's bigger goal. In a world where anyone can build anything, the strategists win.

So we start every project with the end in mind. We get very clear on what success actually looks like. 

Then we use simple project management to finish the thing.

Here's the part that drives me crazy.

33% of the founders I meet are handing their team decision-making power over the company's future. With zero practical frameworks.

25% of our engagements start the same way. Figuring out what mess we have to clean up first.

Projects that led to nothing.

Initiatives left half-built.

Builds with zero strategy and zero awareness of the bottom line.

I'm fed up with it. It's dumb. And it's completely avoidable.

So I wrote a handbook for founders and the people running projects inside their companies.

Think of it as: how to not F up your company with an AI project. For dummies.

If you've got team members running internal AI projects, or you're a non-technical founder running one yourself, you need to read this.

It covers:
→ How to pick the one project that actually moves profit (not the shiny one your team wants to build)
→ How to scope it so it can't end up half-built
→ How to run point on the build without writing a line of code
→ How to run bigger custom builds so they finish instead of sprawl
→ How to audit every project and kill the dead ones before they bleed you

Comment TEAM and I'll send it to you.
(must be following for DM to send)

text:
This is hard part nobody talks about as a SaaS founder...

In the beginning, you're used to doing everything in the company.

Development work, sales, outbound, marketing, customer support, operations, finances, etc.

As you grow, you start hiring people specialized for those roles, but it's still hard to take your hands off the reins.

When I first brought in developers to lead development/project planning on Lead Oracle AI, I was constantly still in the weeds of the codebase.

I remember asking my development agency friends, and they told me I needed to let go of the reins.

I was so bogged down in the day-to-day that I told my development team, I will just be there on our daily standup to be kept in the loop instead of working in the codebase and shipping.

They agreed and took over.

Decisions started being made independently of me. Code was still shipping. Features were still being rolled out.

And I didn't even touch the codebase once.

As a technical founder, it's very easy to become nit-picky.

But at a certain point, you need to let go of the reins slowly and slowly and just simply let your team COOK.

If you're unable to do that, you need either:
1. Better training
2. Better team members that can work independently

Even if it takes 200 interviews to find that one A-player, it's worth it in the end.

text:
AI won’t replace everyone… yet.

But it will do something arguably worse.

It will take the people who already have an advantage - AND MAKE THEM UNTOUCHABLE.

This one is already happening.

Think about it: the prompt a seasoned marketing expert types into Claude is not the same prompt Emeka types when he’s still figuring out what a funnel is. The output isn’t the same. The implementation isn’t the same. The results aren’t the same.

A technical founder building with AI and Amaka launching her first website with AI are not having the same experience. They’re not even playing the same game.

And the pricing gap makes it worse. I’m on the premium plan for almost every AI tool I use. What I can do in an hour, someone on the free tier can’t replicate in a day.

This is what people are missing: EFFORT IS BEING AMPLIFIED NOT REPLACED.

The hard worker is now producing like a team. The expert is now producing like an agency. The already-wealthy are compounding faster than ever.

You don’t notice it because it’s gradual. But gradual doesn’t mean slow - it means invisible until the gap is too wide to cross.

AI isn’t coming for your job (yet)

It’s arming the people ahead of you with everything they need to make sure you never catch up.

text:
Every day for the next long while, I'm going to tear down a new public software company and highlight the AI risks/opportunities around it- products launched to date, top startups, key quotes from earnings calls, etc.

Day two, HubSpot:

Peak share price: $841 (November 12th, 2021)
Share price today: $232 (-72%)
EV today: $ 10.9bn
ARR today: $3.2bn (+21% Y/y)
NRR: 103%
EV/ARR: 3.4x
GAAP Operating Margin: 1.4%
EV/Run-rate GAAP EBIT: 243x
Headcount: 12,234 (+21% Y/y)

AI bear case:

AI-native CRM/marketing automation startups that are natively built around agents as users disrupt HubSpot's core businesses as the value of HubSpot's UI dissipates. GTM moves to something more automated/mechanized vs. being a human endeavor. Seat count declines as AI automates sales/marketing jobs, which leads to secular pressure.

AI bull case:

AI-native CRM companies are still operating off of the same primitives (building GUIs, etc.). HubSpot has a broad platform (Martech, Support, CRM) which will drive  customer stickiness. HubSpot's team is world class, including technical founder @dharmesh, and will keep the company at the cutting edge of agent adoption. SMB customers are much less likely to vibecode their tools than enterprise customers.

AI traction:

Non-disclosed, but business has re-accelerated for the last two quarters and is layering in AI usage credits.

Adjacent startup summary:

Clay- 1090 employees, +77% (not directly competitive)
Unify- 191 employees, +195%
Attio- 142 employees, +80%
Reevo- 98 employees, +250%
Clarify- 35 employees, +150%
Rox- 76 employees, +192%

Management Quotes:

"As I shared last quarter, we expect to see a step-up in net revenue retention in Q4, resulting in a couple of point improvement in net revenue retention for the full year of 2025"

"Customer agent now has over 6,200 customers, up 48% from last quarter with an average resolution rate in the 60s. Prospecting agents has been activated by 6,400 customers, up 94% from last quarter, and customers have used it to engage over 1 million prospects."

"And specifically, with AI, we see the opportunity to monetize both through seats as well as credits. Now core seats, which we talked about at Analyst Day, it is becoming more valuable, and it is embedded with AI data platform value, and that opens up a large opportunity. credits gives us a new way to monetize usage for customers as they consume more AI and agent-driven actions."

Additional Commentary:

Prima facie, HubSpot was very well situated in a maturing SaaS market given its status as a consolidating platform spanning marketing, sales and CX. Given that, it's hard to argue that any one startup is effectively challenging the core business. Mid-market positioning makes it less likely that customers will internally build their own applications. The key question for HubSpot is whether white collar/marketing/sales work is automated writ large by agents in a way that elminates the need for software entirely, especially if HubSpot loses that market to an upstart.

Technical founder learning Marketing 101

I've learned the hard way how important it is to be more active on socials if you're trying to grow a product. I've had several users reach out to me after going through this flow:

1. Hear about my product either from friends or online
2. Check out the product X or Linkedin page
3. See that the last post was 1/2 months ago
4. Assume that the product is abandoned and leave

Even though we ship new features almost every week, most users only glance at the social media pages and don't check the changelog on the website.

Sounds so obvious and yet it took me more than a year to figure out

text:
2025 Wrapped: Lessons learned from a year of making mistakes and trying to learn from them👇

1. Good IX/UI is harder than working code, because users are irrational.  

2. Write your own social media copy.  Don’t just copy-paste AI slop and expect fame and fortune.  

3. It’s OK to refuse to work with nasty  people. 

4. You don’t need to raise VC to build good software.

5. Build a personal brand.  Having a strong personal brand beats a $1,000,000 marketing budget.  

6. Build and write for an audience of people you like.

7. Bootstrapping can be a superpower.  But only if you know the art form. 

8. Statistically, VC’s are counting on your startup to fail.  You deserve better.  

9. Kill passion projects if they’re distracting you from bigger and better things.  

10. Capture social proof when the happy moments occur.  If you wait, it’s too late.

11. Don’t overthink your stack.  NoCode and AI coding tools can take you from MVP to launch if you learn to use them properly.

12. If you’re feeling stuck, take a walk.   Breathe.  Put your phone away.  

13. E-mail is dead.  Please don’t email me if you actually want something.  

14. Success is a vector.  Both speed and direction matter.   

15. Build simple tools that solve your own pains and problems.  

16. Perfection is a trap. Shipping and distribution count more. So ship ugly product. Then fix what users complain about.

17. It’s not a failure if you learned from the experience.  Failure is doing the same dumb thing over and over and expecting different results.  

18. Inaction is fear in disguise.  Or laziness. But usually fear.  

19. Let’s be real: you’re not building the next https://t.co/hJJLvL1qKd.  Also, that doesn’t matter.  Just be honest and humble about what you’re building.  

20. Set your iPhone to greyscale if you spend too much time on it.   And you probably do.  

21. Ideas are cheap, and software is easy to build.  But it’s hard to build, launch and grow a real business.  

22. User feedback that is both real and actionable is hard to acquire.  

23. “Learn by doing” really means “learn from your mistakes.”  So don’t be afraid of making them.  

24. The body does not recover without rest.   Nor does the mind.  But you’ve got to work pretty hard to deserve rest of either kind.  

If you’re a bootstrapped, solo, and/or non-technical founder or business owner, and this resonated, let’s chat in the new year.

text:
How to do reach outs as a technical founder?

In a day, we got an enterprise paying customer for our platform (a YC backed company).

As a hardcore tech guy who likes to stay in silence, draw diagrams, and write code, reaching out people and asking them to checkout your product and converge felt very hard.

My cofounder, a marketing expert, gave me a step by step process.

First of all, we had an ideal ICP in your mind.

For us, it was B2B founders working on enterprise software solutions.

We went on LinkedIn profiles of each founders, and messaged them with a nice greeting message, not sales but asking for insights and some look into the product.

We did this with almost 30 founders (which is less but my LinkedIn got frozen after that)

We got 2 responses, of which, one was interested and schedule a call right away.

In 1 hour, we talked with him and closed at the same moment. 

Again, a good product makes marketing much easier. 

What we are doing right now? 

We follow up consistently, after 2-3 days intervals, because these are busy founders and getting your message buried under a lot of DMs is very easy. 

So showing up and asking 2-3 follow ups is necessary.

Nobody owes you anything that they will get back to you in one attempt.

Also, using tools like Google Sheets is enough to set up a systematic routine.

PS. I share my learning on the way which I learn as a technical founder. I have an awesome marketing cofounder and she helps me a lot while understanding these concepts, which I think a lot of technical nerds need. These might be simple processes for some people but I'm sure it will help some people.

text:
A creator messaged me last week:

“I post every day but nothing grows.
What am I doing wrong?”
So I asked:

“Why are you posting?”

He said:
“To grow.”

Fair answer. But wrong starting point.
So I asked again:

“Who are you posting for?”

Silence.

He didn’t have a person in mind.
He had an algorithm in mind.

So I told him this 👇

The algorithm doesn’t reward consistency.
 People do.
People follow when they feel:

Understood

Helped
Less alone

So I asked him:

“What question do people ask you again and again?”

He said:
“How do I get my first users?”

Boom. That’s the content.

Not:
“Here are 5 growth hacks.”

But:
“Here’s how I got my first users — and what I tried that didn’t work.”

We rewrote one of his posts together.
Instead of:
“Growth is important. You should focus on distribution.”

We changed it to:

“I wasted 3 months building before talking to users.
Here’s what I wish I did instead…”
Same knowledge.
Different framing.

One feels like advice.
The other feels like a story you want to reply to.
Before he left, I told him:

Don’t ask "What should I post today" ?

Ask “What did someone struggle with today that I can help with?”

That’s your content.
Now I want to hear from you:

What’s a question you keep getting?
Or what’s something you struggled with recently?

quote.text:
How to get the first 100 users for your SaaS

You should be able to get 5-10 users organically, posting on Reddit, X, and reaching out to people in your network

They are the key to it all

Reach out and setup a tight feedback loop with them

You want them to tell you whats good but more importantly, whats bad

Give them referral links, they will share the product because of your relationship with them

On top of this, continue the organic methods, trying to have a tight relationship with the first 100 users

Give them all referral links, provide incentives for them to share it with people in their network

Even give the people that are using the referral links incentives to signup

This method obviously doesn't scale well and thats the point

You are building a community that is passionate about the product and is giving you all the feedback you need
